hej med dig.explanation: "Hej med dig" means "hi there". When you leave, it also means "bye": "Hej med dig, vi ses!" (Bye, see you!). To greet several people, say "hej med jer" (hi to you all): "Hej med jer!" (Hi to you all!).

hejsa.explanation: "Hejsa" means "hi there". It is an informal, cheerful version of "hej" (hi). To greet someone and ask how they are: "Hejsa, hvordan har du det?" (Hi there, how are you?).

hektisk.explanation: "Hektisk" means "hectic". Before a word that takes "et", it does not add "t": "et hektisk liv" (a hectic life). With several things, it adds "e": "hektiske tider" (hectic times).

hel.explanation: "Hel" means "whole". To say a whole thing, put it before the noun: "en hel kage" (a whole cake). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helt æble" (a whole apple). To say "the whole day", use "hele": "hele dagen" (the whole day). When something is not broken, it also means "unbroken": "Koppen er hel" (The cup is unbroken).

helbred.explanation: "Helbred" means "health". To say someone's health is poor, put "dårligt" (poor) before it: "Han har dårligt helbred" (He has poor health). Do not mix it up with "sund" (healthy), which describes food: "sund mad" (healthy food).

held.explanation: "Held" means "luck". It is the first word in the phrase "held og lykke" (good luck): "Held og lykke med eksamen" (Good luck with the exam).

heldig.explanation: "Heldig" means "lucky". It comes from "held" (luck), as does "heldigvis" (fortunately). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et heldigt valg" (a lucky choice).

heldigvis.explanation: "Heldigvis" means "fortunately". To say you are glad about how something turned out: "Heldigvis er det fredag" (Fortunately it is Friday). The opposite is "desværre" (unfortunately): "Desværre har jeg ikke tid" (Unfortunately I do not have time).

hele tiden.explanation: "Hele tiden" means "all the time". Literally, it is "the whole time". To say "always", use "altid" (always): "Han kommer altid til tiden" (He always arrives on time).

heller.explanation: "Heller" means "either", as in "not either". To say yes to the same thing, use "også" (too): "Jeg kan også komme" (I can come too). To say no, use "heller ikke": "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

hellere.explanation: "Hellere" means "rather". With "må" (must) it means "had better": "Du må hellere gå nu" (You had better go now). Do not mix it up with "heller" (either): "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

hellere end.explanation: "Hellere end" means "rather than". To say which choice you take and which you skip, name the one you take first: "Jeg tager toget hellere end bilen" (I take the train rather than the car). To say "better late than never": "Hellere sent end aldrig" (literally, "rather late than never").

hellig.explanation: "Hellig" means "sacred". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helligt sted" (a holy place). It is also the first part of "helligdag" (public holiday), literally "holy day".

helst.explanation: "Helst" means "preferably". To say what you would like most: "Jeg vil helst blive hjemme" (I would most like to stay home). To say you would rather not: "Skal du med?" "Helst ikke." (Are you coming? Preferably not.)

helt.explanation: "Helt" means "completely". To say something is complete, put it before the word: "Jeg er enig" (I agree) becomes "Jeg er helt enig" (I completely agree).

hemmelig.explanation: "Hemmelig" means "secret". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmeligt sted" (a secret place). The noun is "en hemmelighed" (a secret): "Det er en hemmelighed" (It is a secret).

hemmelighedsfuld.explanation: "Hemmelighedsfuld" means "secretive". It is built from "en hemmelighed" (a secret) and "-fuld" (full of). The ending "-fuld" also appears in "hensynsfuld" (considerate). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmelighedsfuldt smil" (a secretive smile).

hen.explanation: "Hen" means "over", as in moving over to a place. When someone moves to a place, use it with the verb: "Gå hen til døren" (Walk over to the door). For where someone already is, use "henne" (over there): "Han står henne ved døren" (He stands over there by the door).

hende.explanation: "Hende" means "her". When a woman receives the action, use "hende": "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her). When the woman does the action, use "hun" (she): "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "hende": "Jeg går med hende" (I am going with her).

hendes.explanation: "Hendes" means "her". When the owner is a woman other than the one doing the action, use "hendes": "Anna vasker hendes bil" (Anna washes another woman's car). To say the woman's own, use "sin": "Anna vasker sin bil" (Anna washes her own car).

hensynsfuld.explanation: "Hensynsfuld" means "considerate". It is built from "et hensyn" (a consideration) and "-fuld" (full of). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hensynsfuldt svar" (a considerate answer).

her.explanation: "Her" means "here". To say where you are: "Jeg står her" (I am standing here). For a place away from you, use "der" (there): "Du står der" (You are standing there). Do not mix it up with the English word "her", which is "hende" in Danish: "Jeg ser hende" (I see her).

herfra.explanation: "Herfra" means "from here". It is built from her (here) and fra (from). For a place away from you, use "derfra" (from there): "Det er langt derfra" (It is far from there).

herhen.explanation: "Herhen" means "here", when someone moves toward the speaker. To say someone walks toward the speaker: "Hun går herhen" (She walks here). To say where someone already is, use "her" (here): "Jeg er her" (I am here).
